extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) handling affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131/1.132 to overcome pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejections
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing, evaluating, and using affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 (and related 1.132 practice) to antedate references or activities and overcome pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejections, including who may file, what must be shown, and genus/species issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different inventive entity with at least one common inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: When subject matter disclosed in a patent or patent application publication (reference) naming an inventive entity including joint inventor S and another joint inventor is claimed in a later application naming sole inventor S without the joint inventor, the reference may be properly applied under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (e), or (f) until overcome by an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) showing prior invention or by an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 traversing the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An unequivocal declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 by S that S conceived or invented the subject matter that was disclosed but not claimed in the patent or application publication and relied on in the rejection has been sufficient to overcome the rejection. However, an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 that is only a naked assertion of inventorship by an (joint) inventor who has an interest at stake and that fails to provide any context, explanation or evidence to support that assertion is insufficient. Where the reference is a U.S. patent or patent application publication which includes a claim reciting the subject matter relied upon, a declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 must also explain the presence of the additional joint inventor in the reference (e.g., explain which claims each inventor contributed to). Testimony or disclaimer from the other joint inventor(s) is usually not required but, if submitted, should be considered by the examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common assignee does not obviate affidavit requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact that the reference patent or application publication and the application under examination are owned by the same assignee does not avoid the necessity of filing an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a), in the absence of a showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that the patentee derived the subject matter from the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common ownership does not give the assignee rights to antedate without the required evidence. Where a rejection is applied under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f)/103 or 102(g)/103, or under pre‑AIA 102(e)/103 in certain later‑filed applications, a showing that the invention was commonly owned or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person at the time the later invention was made may preclude or overcome the rejection (see cited MPEP §§ 2146.01–2146.02). For current AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 practice see other sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference is publication of inventor’s own invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 based on a publication may be overcome by a showing that it was published either by the inventor, at least one joint inventor, or on behalf of the inventor or at least one joint inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because such a showing is not made to show a date of invention under 37 CFR 1.131(a), the limitation in pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 104 and in 37 CFR 1.131(a) that only acts occurring in this country or in a NAFTA or WTO member country may be relied on to establish a date of invention is not applicable. Affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 may also be used to show that the reference is a publication of the inventor’s or a joint inventor’s own invention to overcome a rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co‑authorship disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the inventor or at least one joint inventor is a co‑author of a publication cited against an application, a rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or (e) based on the publication may be overcome by filing an affidavit or declaration of the inventor or at least one joint inventor under 37 CFR 1.131(a), or alternatively by filing a specific affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 establishing that the publication is describing work of the inventor or joint inventor(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An uncorroborated affidavit or declaration by a sole inventor or single joint inventor indicating that person to be the sole inventor and the other co‑authors to have been merely working under their direction has been sufficient to remove the publication as a reference in some cases (In re Katz). However, an affidavit or declaration that is only a naked assertion and lacks context, explanation, or corroborating evidence is insufficient (see EmeraChem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation (pre‑AIA context)
rubrics_metrics.description: To remove a rejection where the unclaimed subject matter of a patent, application publication, or other publication is the inventor’s or at least one joint inventor’s own invention, submit evidence establishing that the patentee, applicant of the published application, or author derived their knowledge of the relevant subject matter from the inventor or at least one joint inventor, and that the inventor or joint inventor made the invention upon which the relevant disclosure is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation as discussed here is in the pre‑AIA context. See MPEP §§ 2132.01, 2136.05, and 2137 for related practice and AIA derivation proceedings are discussed elsewhere (MPEP § 2310 et seq.). Case law such as In re Mathews and In re Facius illustrate the requirement to show actual derivation and prior invention by the asserted inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activities applied against the claims (prior use/knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless it is a statutory bar, a rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 based on an activity showing that the claimed invention was used or known prior to the filing date may be overcome by an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) establishing a date of invention prior to the activity or by a specific affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing that the activity was performed by the inventor or at least one joint inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits under 1.131(a) are used to antedate activities by establishing an inventor's earlier date of invention; 1.132 is used to attribute the activity to the inventor or joint inventor. Statutory bars cannot be removed by these showings.

rubrics_metrics.name: How much of the claimed invention must be shown
rubrics_metrics.description: The 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit or declaration must establish possession of either the whole invention claimed or something falling within the claim (such as a species of a claimed genus), in the sense that the claim as a whole reads on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If differences between the claimed invention and the disclosure of the reference(s) are so small as to render the claims obvious over the reference(s), an affidavit or declaration may be required to show no more than the reference shows (In re Stryker). An affidavit need not show identical disclosure; what matters is 'how much the reference shows of the claimed invention.' The affidavit must establish possession of the basic inventive concept, not merely of what a particular reference happens to show. Examples and case law (Tanczyn, Clarke, Spiller, Wakefield) illustrate these principles. Even if the affidavit is not fully commensurate with the rejected claim, the applicant can overcome the rejection by showing that the differences would have been obvious in view of the affidavit evidence prior to the effective date of the reference(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Swearing behind one of a plurality of combined references
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may overcome a pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejection based on a combination of references by showing completion of the invention by the inventor prior to the effective date of any of the references; the applicant need not antedate the reference with the earliest prior art date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit must show possession of the whole invention as claimed or something within the claim before the prior art date of the reference being antedated; it is not enough to show possession merely of what one reference shows if that reference does not teach the basic inventive concept. Where Reference A is rejected in view of Reference B, applicant can rely on teachings of Reference B to show the differences would have been obvious before Reference A's date, but must still establish possession of the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule as to generic claims (antedating genus by species)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference or activity applied against generic claims may (in most cases) be antedated as to such claims by an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) showing completion of the invention of only a single species within the genus before the prior art date of the reference or activity (assuming the reference/activity is not a statutory bar or a patent/application publication claiming the same invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle (Ex parte Biesecker) is subject to exceptions in unpredictable arts; see MPEP § 715.03 for practice relative to cases in unpredictable arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus‑Species: Species claim (overcoming reference that discloses a species)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the claim under rejection recites a species and the reference or activity discloses the claimed species, the rejection can be overcome under 37 CFR 1.131(a) directly by showing prior completion of the claimed species or indirectly by showing prior completion of a different species coupled with a showing that the claimed species would have been an obvious modification of the species completed by the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (In re Spiller, In re Clarke, In re Plumb, In re Hostettler) illustrates that proof of prior completion of a different species can suffice if the claimed species would have been obvious from what the inventor had made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus‑Species: Genus claim (when disclosure shows species only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the only pertinent disclosure in the reference or activity is a single species of the claimed genus, the applicant can overcome the rejection directly under 37 CFR 1.131(a) by showing the inventor's prior possession of the species disclosed in the reference or activity. Conversely, a reference disclosing several species of a claimed genus can be overcome directly under 37 CFR 1.131(a) only by showing that the inventor completed, prior to the date of the reference or activity, all of the species shown in the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of prior completion of a species different from the species of the reference can be sufficient indirectly if the species shown in the reference would have been obvious in view of the species shown to have been made by the inventor. Alternatively, an applicant may antedate indirectly by showing prior completion of enough species to place the inventor in possession of the claimed genus. The test is whether the species completed provide an adequate basis for inferring generic applicability (In re Plumb, In re Rainer, In re Clarke, In re Shokal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Species versus embodiments (single invention embodiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: References or activities which disclose one or more embodiments of a single claimed invention can be overcome by filing a 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit showing prior completion of a single embodiment of the invention, whether it is the same or a different embodiment from that disclosed in the reference or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish embodiments of a single invention from genus/species disclosures. In genus/species contexts, it is necessary that the species reduced to practice provide an adequate basis for inferring that the invention has generic applicability (In re DaFano). Example: where the inventive concept is the use of a material for a function (e.g., PVP as soil‑suspending agent), differing detergents may be viewed as different embodiments of the same invention rather than distinct species of a genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference discloses claimed genus (predictability concerns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the reference or activity discloses the claimed genus, a showing of completion of a single species within the genus is generally sufficient to antedate the reference or activity under 37 CFR 1.131(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases where predictability is in question, however, a showing of prior completion of one or a few species within the disclosed genus is generally not sufficient. The test is whether the species completed provide an adequate basis for inferring that the invention has generic applicability. The number of species needed depends on the size and predictability of the genus (e.g., small genus may require fewer species; large genus may require many). Case law (Shokal, Mantell, Rainer, DeFano, Clarke, Schaub) provides guidance: '[I]n the case of a small genus ... a reduction to practice of three, or perhaps even two, might serve to complete the generic invention, while in the case of a genus comprising hundreds of species, a considerably larger number of reductions to practice would probably be necessary.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may make affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations filed under 37 CFR 1.131 to overcome a rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 must be made by specified parties: (A) The entire inventive entity (i.e., the inventor). (B) Less than all named joint inventors if it is shown that less than all named joint inventors invented the subject matter of the claim(s) under rejection. (C) For applications filed before Sept 16, 2012, a joint inventor or assignee under pre‑AIA 37 CFR 1.47 if a petition under 1.47 was granted or the application was accepted under pre‑AIA 1.42 or 1.43. (D) For applications filed before Sept 16, 2012, the legal representative of a deceased, insane or otherwise legally incapacitated sole inventor, or joint inventor in certain cases. (E) For applications filed on or after Sept 16, 2012, the party qualified under 37 CFR 1.42 or 1.46. (F) The assignee or other party in interest when it is not possible to produce the affidavit or declaration of the sole inventor, or joint inventor when item (B) applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the listed categories carefully depending on application filing date and applicable pre‑AIA rules. Case citation: Ex parte Foster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing under wrong rule treated as 1.132
rubrics_metrics.description: Although affidavits or declarations submitted for the purpose of establishing that the reference discloses the inventor’s or at least one joint inventor’s invention are properly filed under 37 CFR 1.132, such affidavits submitted improperly under 37 CFR 1.131(a) will be considered as though they were filed under 37 CFR 1.132 to traverse a ground of rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner/practitioner should be aware that misfiling does not necessarily discard the evidence but will change its legal effect and the type of showing required. See In re Facius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency and corroboration of affidavits/declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration that is only a naked assertion of inventorship by an (joint) inventor who has an interest at stake and that fails to provide any context, explanation or evidence to support that assertion is insufficient to show that the relied‑upon subject matter was the work of the inventive entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits/declarations should provide factual context, explanation, and, where appropriate, corroborating evidence (e.g., drawings, contemporaneous records, testimony) to lend credence. Timing and circumstances matter: affidavits submitted decades after the invention without supporting context have been found insufficient (see EmeraChem). While some uncorroborated affidavits have sufficed in particular cases, reliance on naked or conclusory statements is risky.
